extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and the moral/social sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for forming and evaluating arguments, evidence, and reasoning in moral and social science inquiry (with attention to common fallacies). Useful for reviewers, students, and practitioners assessing argument validity and method choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begging the Question (Petitio Principii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid assuming in the premises the very point which is to be proved (the conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: arguments that assume the impossibility of a minimum (infinite divisibility example); formulations that make the premise seem more obvious than the conclusion though they are identical. The fallacy often appears as a plausible but circular verbal juggle; check whether the premise really requires independent proof rather than covertly restating the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity / Equivocation (Ambiguous middle-term)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect and eliminate cases where a term changes meaning between premises and conclusion (the middle term is ambiguous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using ‘something’ in one premise to mean a substance and in another to mean any object of thought. When a term is used in different senses the argument may appear valid while actually failing; resolve ambiguous terms or restate premises with precise meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori fallacy / Natural prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer non-existence from inability to conceive; avoid treating what is inconceivable as therefore impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called the 'a priori' fallacy in the text: arguments that appeal to the incapacity of imagination (e.g., to conceive a minimum) are merely appeals to prejudice, not demonstration. Be wary when premises rely on intuitive inconceivability rather than empirical or logical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrelevant Conclusion (Ignoratio Elenchi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that the proposition proved is the very proposition required, and not some different or only practically similar proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whately's examples: substituting the particular for the universal, or proving a different proposition that serves a similar emotional purpose. Sophistical tactics include proving a related but distinct point which excites the desired disposition rather than establishing the target claim. Reviewers should check that the argument’s conclusion matches the issue in dispute, not a sidetrack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper appeal to emotion / passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from using emotional effect or rhetorical devices as substitutes for proof of the proposition in issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: making an audience laugh to undercut an opponent’s defense; using odious labels ('rogue') to overwhelm mitigating facts. Such appeals may achieve practical persuasion but do not establish the logical point; flag these as irrelevant when they replace substantive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation of the opponent (proving what was not asserted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attribute to your opponent opinions or propositions they have not held, and do not refute a position they never advanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignoratio Elenchi often manifests as disproving or denying what was never asserted. This is both unfair and logically irrelevant. In reviews and debates check whether criticisms actually address the author's stated claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match evidence to the kind of claim (distinguish phenomenon from noumenon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate kinds of evidence for the claim’s ontological level; sensory evidence cannot answer metaphysical claims about hidden substrata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Berkeley’s denial of matter concerns the substratum or hidden cause of sensations; appealing to sense-data (knocking a stick) misses the point. Reviewers must ensure evidence targets the same conceptual level as the claim (appearances vs supposed hidden causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not construct principles of evidence or method purely a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles of evidence and theories of scientific method should be inferred from observing how reasoning and inquiry actually succeed, not solely from abstract deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The laws of our rational faculty are 'only learned by seeing the agent at work.' Historical and practical success (e.g., Bacon) should guide methodological prescriptions. Reviewers should favor empirically grounded methodological rules over purely speculative ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalize judiciously from simple to complex cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive methods by observing successful practice in simpler problems and then adapt them, with care, to the greater complexities of moral and social inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that we 'learn to do a thing in difficult circumstances by attending to the manner in which we have spontaneously done the same thing in easier ones.' In evaluating methodology, check whether the author appropriately adapts techniques proven in simpler sciences to the moral/social domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms precisely; avoid misleading terminology (e.g., 'Necessity')
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose clear, appropriate terms to express causal or theoretical claims; avoid words whose common sense connotations distort understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the term 'Necessity' carries implications of irresistibleness and can induce fatalistic associations. The text recommends abandoning objectionable terms that invite misinterpretation. Peer reviewers should insist on lexical clarity where ordinary associations could mislead readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize causation in human action as predictive yet open to countervailing causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When explaining human behavior, treat motives and character as determinants that allow prediction if known, while acknowledging that causes are not uncontrollable and other causes may intervene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical Necessity (as used in the text) means predictability given motives and character, not mystical compulsion. Reviewers should ensure causal claims recognize the possibility of counteraction and do not implicitly assert fatalistic inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for agents' capacity for self-formation (feedback and intervention)
rubrics_metrics.description: In social and moral theorizing include the capacity of individuals to alter their own character by willingly adopting means that reshape dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that people can 'place ourselves under the influence of other circumstances' and thus form character by will. Methodological accounts should model such feedback loops rather than treating character as utterly fixed by antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize non-instrumental motives and the role of habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce all motives to conscious anticipations of pleasure or pain; account for actions that become desired and performed for their own sake through association and habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes actions can become ends in themselves, performed without reference to expected pleasure. Explanatory models of motivation should therefore allow habitual, non-instrumental desires and not simplistically map every action to a calculated pleasure/pain calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure empirical evidence actually addresses the asserted universal claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating particular or exceptional facts as refutations of universal or qualified generalizations by addressing the wrong target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malthus example: showing population stationary in some places does not refute his qualified claim about tendency to increase when unrestrained. Reviewers must check that cited empirical instances truly bear on the general claim and that the scope/qualifications of the generalization are respected.
